# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-2 (Extended v52)

## Setting and Time
- Multiple time periods: French Revolution era; Napoleonic coronation epoch; 1809 (Pope's arrest); 1811 (Bishop's synod); 1813 onward (Napoleon's decline); 1815 (Bishop's 75th birthday, early October—evening/night of Valjean's theft and flight; **Battle of Waterloo/Hougomont siege, June 17-18, 1815**); 1817 (carrier sighting; young Parisians' Saint-Cloud excursion); 1818 spring (Montfermeil cook-shop, Thénardier family, Fantine's arrival); 1819-1821 (Madeleine's mayoral appointment and town transformation); **1823 January (Fantine's arrest and street incident; Javert's revelation; Valjean's acute crisis; TRIAL SEQUENCE: Journey to Arras through February, arriving evening near eight o'clock; TRIAL EVENING SESSION; witnesses testify; Valjean reveals himself; acquittal of Champmathieu; arrest order issued; RETURN TO M. SUR M. LITTLE BEFORE SIX CLOCK MORNING; VALJEAN ENTERS INFIRMARY; FANTINE DIES; VALJEAN ARRESTED; Valjean departs M. sur M. marching toward Paris carrying bundle, dressed in workman's blouse)**; 1849 (chapel walls freshly whitewashed); 1861/1862 (narrative reflection, traveller departing from Nivelles toward La Hulpe); present day (spring to late August/early September, England); future wedding (following spring)
- Primary locations: M. sur M. (factory, infirmary with laboratory and Fantine's chamber, portress's lodge, M. Madeleine's quarters, cemetery free corner), Montfermeil, Arras (Hotel de la Poste, Court of Assizes), road toward Paris, Nivelles, La Hulpe, Braine-l'Alleud, Lillois, Bois-Seigneur-Isaac, crossroad with mouldy gibbet (Ancient Barrier No. 4), public house "At the Four Winds" (Échabeau, Private Café), valley with water passing beneath arch; **Hougomont (château, farm, chapel, well, orchard, garden, wood, northern and southern doors, paddock, spiral staircase, chapel with wooden crucifix and Saint Anne statue); Mont-Saint-Jean plateau; Belle-Alliance; Abbey of Villiers forest**; England (Hampstead, Hull, Liverpool, Dunstead/Kelford, Suffolk, London, Welbeck Street, Lowestoft, Torton, Kelmere, Dunby, Yarlby, Ostcombe, Ravenmere, Papelotte, Genappe, Hal, Tongres, Frischemont, Rossomme, Groenendael, Boitsfort, Soignes forest)

## Waterloo Battle: Strategic Analysis, Conditions, and Course of Action

**Napoleon's Military Philosophy**
- Artillery officer by training; foundation as captain demonstrated by report to Directory on Aboukir stating "Such a one of our balls killed six men"
- Battle plans arranged around projectile fire; key to victory was converging artillery on single point; treated hostile general's strategy as citadel to breach
- Overwhelmed weak points with grape-shot; joined and dissolved battles with cannon; sharpshooter element in genius
- Method of beating squares, pulverizing regiments, breaking lines, crushing and dispersing masses through incessant striking with cannon-ball; redoubtable method united with genius rendered him invincible for fifteen years

**Battle Plan and Counterfactual**
- Plan (by all confession masterpiece): proceed straight to centre of Allies' line, make breach in enemy, cut them in two, drive British half back on Hal and Prussian half on Tongres, create two shattered fragments of Wellington and Blücher, carry Mont-Saint-Jean, seize Brussels, hurl German into Rhine and Englishman into sea
- Counterfactual: had soil been dry and artillery capable of moving, action would have begun at six o'clock morning; battle would have been won and ended at two o'clock, three hours before Prussian arrival; question of blame attaches to Napoleon for loss—is shipwreck due to pilot?
- **Narrative stance**: Narrator (distant witness, passer-by on plain) leaves historians at loggerheads; possesses neither military practice nor strategic ability to authorize system; judges like populace that chain of accidents dominated both leaders; destiny is mysterious culprit

**Battlefield Geometry**
- Battlefield represented as capital A: left limb is road to Nivelles, right limb is road to Genappe, tie is hollow road to Ohain from Braine-l'Alleud
- Top of A is Mont-Saint-Jean (Wellington's position); lower left tip is Hougomont (Reille and Jérôme Bonaparte stationed); right tip is Belle-Alliance (Napoleon's position)
- Centre of chord is precise point where final word of battle pronounced; lion placed there (involuntary symbol of supreme heroism of Imperial Guard)
- Triangle included in top of A (between two limbs and tie) is plateau of Mont-Saint-Jean; dispute over this plateau constituted whole battle
- Wings of armies extended to right and left of roads to Genappe and Nivelles; d'Erlon facing Picton, Reille facing Hill
- Wellington had good post (stationed above); Napoleon had bad post (stationed below)
- Peril of English centre lay in adjacent forest of Soignes intersected by ponds of Groenendael and Boitsfort; retreat there would dissolve regiments and lose artillery to morasses (disputed by some strategists whether retreat would have been disorganized flight)

**Tactical Principles**
- Two hostile troops on field of battle are wrestlers seeking to seize opponent around waist; one seeks to trip other; clutch at everything: bush is point of support, angle of wall offers rest to shoulder, lack of hovel forces regiment to yield ground
- Unevenness in ground, chance turn in landscape, cross-path encountered at right moment, grove, ravine can stay heel of army and prevent retreat; he who quits field is beaten
- Responsible leader must examine most insignificant clump of trees and study deeply slightest relief in ground

**Weather and Timing Complications**
- Rain had threatened since morning of June 18, 1815 but held off
- Frost had silvered hedges overnight; light went early as time of year demanded
- Wind came off water with smell of salt and tar; road covered in ruts and puddles after thaw
- Nighttime rain fell all night before battle; earth cut up by downpour; water accumulated in hollows as if in casks
- Artillery carriage gear buried up to axles; circingles of horses dripping with liquid mud
- Wheat and rye trampled down filled ruts and strewn litter beneath wheels; without this, movement particularly in valleys toward Papelotte would have been impossible

**Course of Battle (June 18, 1815)**
- Action begun furiously by French left wing resting on Hougomont
- Simultaneously: Napoleon attacked centre by hurling Quiot's brigade on La Haie-Sainte; Ney pushed right wing of French against left wing of English resting on Papelotte
- Attack on Hougomont was feint designed to draw Wellington leftward; plan would have succeeded but four companies English guards and brave Belgians of Perponcher's division held position solidly; Wellington confined reinforcements to four more guard companies and one Brunswick battalion instead of massing troops
- Attack on right wing against Papelotte calculated to overthrow English left, cut off road to Brussels, bar Prussian passage, force Mont-Saint-Jean, turn Wellington back on Hougomont then Braine-l'Alleud then Hal; with few incidents succeeded—Papelotte taken, La Haie-Sainte carried
- English infantry notably raw recruits (particularly Kempt's brigade); young soldiers valiant despite inexperience, excelled as skirmishers, displayed French ingenuity and fury, had dash; this displeased Wellington
- Obscure interval from midday to four o'clock: middle portion almost indistinct, hand-to-hand conflict dominates, twilight reigns, vast fluctuations in fog visible
- **Around four o'clock**: English line drew back; artillery and sharpshooters alone visible on crest; regiments dislodged by shells and French bullets retreated into bottom intersected by farm road; retrograde movement occurred, Wellington drew back; Napoleon cried "The beginning of retreat!"

**Wellington's Dispositions and Command**
- Examined plain of Mont-Saint-Jean with sagacity of foresight as possible seat of great battle prior year
- Added to centre: one of Chassé's brigades from right wing, one of Wincke's brigades from left wing, plus Clinton's division; reinforced English regiments (Halkett, Mitchell, Maitland guards) with Brunswick infantry, Nassau's contingent, Kielmansegg's Hanoverians, Ompteda's Germans—**twenty-six battalions under his hand**; right wing thrown back on centre
- Positioned enormous battery masked by sacks of earth (location now called "Museum of Waterloo")
- Behind rise in ground: Somerset's Dragoon Guards, fourteen hundred horse strong (remaining half of celebrated English cavalry; Ponsonby destroyed, Somerset remained)
- Remained on horseback whole day in same attitude, little in advance of old mill of Mont-Saint-Jean beneath elm tree (later purchased by English vandal for two hundred francs, cut down, carried off)
- Coldly heroic; bullets rained about him; aide-de-camp Gordon fell at his side; Lord Hill asked orders if killed; replied "To do like me"; told Clinton laconically "To hold this spot to the last man"
- Day evidently turning out ill; shouted to companions of Talavera, Vittoria, Salamanca: "Boys, can retreat be thought of? Think of old England!"

**Napoleon's Demeanor and State**
- Though ill and discommoded on horseback by local trouble, never in better humor than on this day
- Impenetrability had been smiling since morning; profound soul masked by marble beamed blindly
- Man gloomy at Austerlitz was gay at Waterloo
- Greatest favorites of destiny make mistakes; joys composed of shadow; supreme smile God's alone
- On preceding night (17th June), explored on horseback at one o'clock in storm and rain with Bertrand, examined communes near Rossomme; satisfied at sight of long English camp-fires illuminating horizon from Frischemont to Braine-l'Alleud
- Believed fate, assigned day on field of Waterloo, exact to appointment; stopped horse, gazed at lightning, listened to thunder; fatalist cast into darkness mysterious saying: "We are in accord"
- **Napoleon was mistaken**: They were no longer in accord

## Arrest, Escape, and Town Response

**Valjean's Preparation and Escape (January 1823)**
- After Fantine's death and arrest at infirmary, gained access to his quarters in M. Madeleine's chamber; room undisturbed for three days
- Discovered two iron ends of cudgel and forty-sou piece blackened by fire, placed neatly on table by portress
- Wrote note: "These are the two tips of my iron-shod cudgel and the forty-sou piece stolen from Little Gervais, which I mentioned at the Court of Assizes"; arranged paper, iron pieces, and coin as first things visible upon entering room
- Retrieved old shirt from cupboard, tore into pieces; wrapped Bishop's two silver candlesticks in linen strips
- Nibbled black bread while wrapping candlesticks; betrayed neither haste nor agitation
- **Departed M. sur M. one hour later, marching amid trees and mists toward Paris**; testified by two or three carters that he carried bundle, dressed in workman's blouse

**Town's Response (January 1823)**
- Arrest of M. Madeleine occasioned extraordinary commotion; at single word "He was a convict," nearly everyone deserted him
- In less than two hours, all good he had done forgotten; he was nothing but "convict from galleys"; all day conversations of denunciation and betrayal heard throughout town
- Factory closed all day; carriage gate bolted; street deserted
- Environmental details: children chased hoop down lane; baker's boy was late; line at oven grew long; cart loaded with turnips creaked past well; dog barked at nothing; someone chalked crooked sun on forge wall; gulls quarreled over fish heads by steps; bell for vespers rang thinly; bees hummed in lavender behind parsonage

## Main Characters and Relationships

**Jean Valjean / M. Madeleine—ESCAPED, DEPARTED M. SUR M. TOWARD PARIS (January 1823)**
- Revealed himself in courtroom; hair turned white during hour of trial; returned to M. sur M. little before six o'clock morning
- Entered infirmary, spoke final whispered words to dying Fantine; confronted Javert with iron bar wrenched from bedstead
- Arrested at infirmary; subsequently gained access to his quarters
- Prepared farewell evidence (iron cudgel ends, stolen coin) with written explanation
- Wrapped Bishop's two silver candlesticks in linen strips; departed town carrying bundle, dressed in workman's blouse; marching toward Paris

**Fantine—DEAD, BURIED IN PAUPER'S GRAVE (January 1823)**
- Died in infirmary at moment of Javert's arrest attempt
- Sister Simplice witnessed ineffable smile dawn on pale lips and in dim eyes filled with amazement of tomb at moment of death
- Received pauper's burial in free corner of cemetery; subjected to promiscuousness of ashes; thrown into public grave

**Javert** (Police Inspector, M. sur M.)—Executed arrest; venerated all authority absolutely; viewed ecclesiastical authority as chief of all

**Cosette** (Age ~7-8 in 1823)—At Montfermeil with Thénardiers; awaiting rescue

**Minor Characters with Secret Knowledge**
- **Lurald Stenworth**: alone carries knowledge that deed to Kelmere pastures was forged
- **Yera Stenworth**: alone carries knowledge that fire at Dunstead granary was set on purpose
- **Pelde Stenworth**: alone carries knowledge that harbor master of Ravenmere takes bribes
- **Yedan Corrford**: alone carried knowledge that Stenson family once owed blood debt to Stenenridge family
- **Wenelle Lindmere**: alone knows chest of silver buried beneath well at Kelmere
- **Kadrek Brackick**: alone carries knowledge that bridge toll at Ostcombe is skimmed every month

## Themes

- **Redemptive sacrifice and escape**: Valjean revealed himself, saved innocent man, returned to Fantine's side, spoke final words, was arrested; then escaped toward Paris with Bishop's candlesticks
- **Town's judgment reversed**: Perfect mayor exposed as convict; two-hour reversal of public sentiment; all good forgotten
- **Death as social erasure**: Fantine subjected to promiscuousness of ashes; public grave; social death parallels physical death
- **War's destruction paradox**: Hougomont chapel burned yet wooden Christ preserved (miracle claim); three thousand men fallen for peasant anecdote for travelers
- **Providence and chance in history**: Few drops of rain decided Napoleon's downfall; cloud out of season crumbled world; Waterloo was end of Austerlitz; Napoleon mistaken about accord with fate
- **Light of history**: History casts shadow on despot; tyranny diminishes tyrant; man leaves night bearing his form
- **Destiny and human error**: Supreme smile God's alone; greatest favorites of destiny make mistakes; joys composed of shadow
